name: Trafilatura (Python; PyPI `trafilatura`, CLI `trafilatura`), by Adrien Barbaresi (BBAW). Ports and relatives: rs-trafilatura (Rust, Murrough Foley), go-trafilatura (Go, markusmobius), trafilatura-rs bindings. Academic name: 'Trafilatura: A Web Scraping Library and Command-Line Tool for Text Discovery and Extraction' (ACL-IJCNLP 2021 System Demonstrations).
kind: Library plus command-line tool (Python), with independent reimplementations in Rust and Go. rs-trafilatura additionally ships a trained ML page-type classifier, so it is a library with an embedded model artifact rather than a pure rule system.
maturity: Production. Trafilatura is the most widely deployed open-source text extractor in the LLM-corpus pipeline world (used in CommonCrawl-derived pipelines, HuggingFace dataset builds, and as the default extractor in several crawler stacks); version line 2.x as of 2026. rs-trafilatura is early-production: v0.2, tens of stars, single author, 24 commits at time of survey -- adoptable but with an unproven maintenance record and a model artifact whose retraining cadence is undefined.
license: Trafilatura: Apache-2.0 from v1.8.0 onward; GPLv3+ for v1.7.x and earlier. This matters -- pinning an older version silently pulls a copyleft dependency into the project. rs-trafilatura: dual MIT / Apache-2.0. Both permit use here; only the pre-1.8 Trafilatura line does not fit a permissive-only posture.
keeps_and_discards: Trafilatura is a cascade, not a single algorithm. It runs (1) hand-written XPath expressions that positively target likely body containers and negatively discard containers matching nav/footer/comment/aside/share/related patterns, (2) a fallback ladder into readability-lxml and jusText when its own pass yields too little text, and (3) an optional separate comment-extraction pass with its own XPath set. It keeps prose paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, code blocks, quotes and (optionally) comment threads; it discards navigation, footers, sidebars, share widgets, cookie notices matched by pattern, and by default all form controls. Metadata (title, author, date, sitename, categories, tags, license, url) is extracted separately from meta tags, JSON-LD, Open Graph and Dublin Core. rs-trafilatura changes the shape of this: it first classifies the page into one of seven types (article, forum, product, collection, listing, documentation, service) with an XGBoost model of 200 trees over 181 features, then applies a per-type extraction profile. So what is kept is conditioned on a predicted page category -- an explicit region/page-kind classifier, which is the exact thing this project's structure_agnosticism constraint forbids.
structure_preserved: Substantially more than Readability, and this is Trafilatura's real differentiator. Output targets include TXT, CSV, JSON, HTML, Markdown, XML and XML-TEI; the XML/TEI target retains a typed element tree (head, p, list/item, table/row/cell, quote, code, graphic) with nesting and document order, and TEI output carries a teiHeader with the extracted metadata. Tabular relations survive as row/cell structure in the XML and Markdown targets. What does not survive: the ancestor chain above the chosen body container (kept content is reparented into a flat document), any relation between kept and discarded material, attribute-level information other than href/src, and element identity. Shadow boundaries are entirely outside the model -- Trafilatura consumes serialized HTML through lxml, so open shadow roots are absent unless the caller pre-composes them, closed roots are unrepresentable, and there is no unreachable marker for either. rs-trafilatura emits GitHub-Flavored Markdown with headings, lists and tables preserved; it does not emit TEI.
interactive_elements: Discarded as a class. form, input, button, select and textarea are not in the kept element set for any output target; they are neither serialized nor counted. Anchors survive as links in Markdown/HTML/XML targets with hrefs resolved when a base URL is supplied, and images survive as graphic elements when `include_images` is set. There is no notion of a control, an affordance, or an action -- the output is a reading artifact. For a sensor whose purpose is to hand a model something clickable, Trafilatura's output is unusable as-is; only its structural serializer is relevant.
interactive_state_fidelity: Zero, and unrecoverable. disabled, checked, selected, aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-pressed, aria-current and role are dropped with the elements that carry them; aria attributes are read only in the negative direction (aria-hidden participates in discard decisions). The token cost of interactive state in Trafilatura output is exactly zero because the affordance count is zero. This makes Trafilatura a clean negative control for the 'tag plus interactivity' hypothesis: it demonstrates the upper bound of prose compression when affordances are simply deleted, so the difference between its token count and a tag-plus-interactivity fold's token count is a direct measurement of what interactivity costs. Note the asymmetry against the project's measured 80.9% affordance projection: Trafilatura's affordance projection is approximately 0% against the same 99.7% capture, so it cannot be a fidelity baseline, only a compression baseline.
layout_awareness: None geometric anywhere in the pipeline. Trafilatura never has a rendering engine available -- it operates on an lxml tree parsed from bytes -- so getBoundingClientRect, computed style, viewport and stacking context do not exist for it. Its only visibility-adjacent signals are attribute-level: elements with hidden, aria-hidden, or inline display:none patterns are discarded by XPath, and `style` is otherwise ignored. rs-trafilatura's 181 classifier features are structural and lexical counts (tag frequencies, text/link ratios, depth statistics), not geometric. This means both satisfy no_layout_in_the_fold trivially, and both inherit the corresponding weakness: they cannot detect CSS-driven concealment.
javascript_required: No, and this is a hard limitation rather than a design choice. Both operate on static HTML bytes. Client-rendered pages yield the loading skeleton; content behind hydration, infinite scroll, or shadow-DOM-based components is simply absent, and no error is raised. The privacy consequence is favourable -- because no scripts run, no telemetry fires, no beacons are sent, and no third-party resources load during extraction itself -- but only because the fetch already happened elsewhere. In the project's own architecture the browser has already executed the page before the fold runs, so Trafilatura's no-JS property offers no privacy benefit and only costs coverage. WCXB explicitly excluded JavaScript-heavy SPAs from its corpus, which means every Trafilatura ranking in circulation was measured on precisely the page population where its blindness does not show.
evaluation_method: Two mutually incompatible methodologies are in circulation, and they disagree about Trafilatura's rank. (A) Trafilatura's own docs/evaluation.html: a segment-level classification task. 990 documents are pre-segmented into 2,951 text segments and 2,966 boilerplate segments; each tool's output is checked for whether each segment's text is present, giving precision, recall, accuracy and F-score over segments. Because the segment inventory is fixed in advance and roughly balanced, this measures boilerplate discrimination on a curated diet. (B) WCXB (arXiv 2605.21097): word-bag F1. Extracted text and ground truth are both lowercased and split on non-alphanumeric characters into bags of word tokens; F1 is computed over token bags, so word order, structure and duplication are unscored. WCXB additionally reports 'with-snippet recall' (content completeness) and 'without-snippet inclusion' (boilerplate contamination) as separate axes. (C) The ScrapingHub article-extraction-benchmark, 181 article pages, is the third source and is article-only.
corpus_size_and_origins: Trafilatura's own set: 990 documents, drawn from large collections of German web pages, with roughly 20-30% in other languages (English, French, other European languages, Chinese, Arabic). No origin/domain count is published, no sampling frame is stated, and the set has been extended incrementally by the author over years -- it is a curated collection, not a sample. Last run reported 2026-08-04 on Python 3.13. WCXB: 2,008 pages from 1,613 domains, collected September 2025 to March 2026, split 1,497 development / 511 held-out test, seven page types with articles at 53% of the dataset, predominantly English, static snapshots only with SPAs excluded, released CC-BY-4.0 with HTML sources on GitHub/Zenodo/HuggingFace. ScrapingHub: 181 article pages, English news, published 2019 and never refreshed. Every one of these corpora is frozen HTML; none contains a live page, a consent-gated capture, or a shadow-DOM component, so none of them measures the population this project's 136-page live corpus is drawn from.
reported_precision_recall: Trafilatura self-reported (990 docs, 2026-08-04, segment F-score): trafilatura 2.2.0 standard P 0.906 / R 0.943 / accuracy 0.923 / F 0.924 -- first place; magic-html 0.889 F; jusText 3.0.2 custom 0.862 F; news-please 0.836 F; readability-lxml 0.826 F; goose3 0.810 F (highest precision at 0.936, lowest recall at 0.714). WCXB (1,497 dev pages, word-bag F1): rs-trafilatura 0.859; MinerU-HTML 0.827; Resiliparse 0.797; Trafilatura 0.791; dom-smoothie 0.762; ReaderLM-v2 0.741; BoilerPy3 0.687; Readability 0.674. rs-trafilatura on the 511-page held-out test: F1 0.893. ScrapingHub 181 articles: rs-trafilatura F1 0.966 (P 0.942 / R 0.991), go-trafilatura 0.960, Python trafilatura 0.958 (P 0.938 / R 0.978). Per-type on WCXB: Trafilatura article 0.932, documentation 0.932, product 0.670; rs-trafilatura article 0.932, documentation 0.931, service 0.843, forum 0.792, collection 0.713, listing 0.704, product 0.670. Snippet axes: rs-trafilatura with-snippet recall 75.6% / without-snippet inclusion 9.6%; Trafilatura 69.5% recall / 6.6% boilerplate; Resiliparse 74.5% recall / 22.8% boilerplate. THE CONTRADICTION: Trafilatura places 1st at 0.924 in its author's benchmark and 4th at 0.791 in rs-trafilatura's author's benchmark. Both figures are real; neither is independent. The rank inversion is a property of the metric and corpus choice, not of the tools.
independent_oracle: None. Trafilatura's oracle is a segment inventory the author curated; WCXB's oracle is a main-content span drafted by an LLM (Claude), verified by scripts, reviewed across four frontier-model passes, and adjudicated by a single human annotator with no inter-annotator agreement reported. Both oracles encode the same premise the tools encode: that a page has one identifiable main content region separable from boilerplate. On listings, collections and product pages that premise is contested, and the 0.67-0.71 scores there are partly the oracle disagreeing with itself. WCXB's LLM-drafted ground truth carries a second, sharper problem: two of the systems it ranks (MinerU-HTML, ReaderLM-v2) are themselves LLM-based extractors, so the oracle and two contestants share a generative prior. The only oracle-free checks -- recall against the full capture, round-trip fixed point, compression ratio at fixed recall -- are published for neither tool.
evidence_independence: Explicitly not independent, in both directions, and this is the item's central finding. The 0.924 figure that ranks Trafilatura first is produced and published by Trafilatura's own author on a corpus he curated. The 0.859-vs-0.791 figure that ranks rs-trafilatura first and demotes Trafilatura to fourth is produced and published by rs-trafilatura's own author (Murrough Foley) on a corpus he built and annotated, and rs-trafilatura's README quotes it as a headline claim. These are the two most-cited numbers for this tool family and they are mutually contradictory author-run results. The ScrapingHub benchmark is the only corpus here not authored by a competing extractor, and it is article-only, 181 pages, and seven years stale. There is no third-party evaluation of rs-trafilatura at all. Any adoption decision that cites either headline F1 without naming its author is laundering a vendor claim.
page_archetype_coverage: The spread is the story. Trafilatura on WCXB ranges 0.932 (article, documentation) down to 0.670 (product) -- a 26-point spread; rs-trafilatura ranges 0.932 down to 0.670 with the same floor, meaning its +0.068 aggregate advantage comes entirely from the middle types (service 0.843, forum 0.792, listing 0.704) and NOT from the hardest one. Both tools are effectively tied and effectively bad on product pages. WCXB's own finding that article extraction is essentially solved (top systems clustered 0.87-0.93) means the aggregate rank ordering is decided almost entirely by non-article types, which are the minority of the corpus (articles are 53%) and the ones with fewest examples -- so the headline ranking rests on the thinnest per-type samples. For this project, whose targets include listings, search results, forums and product pages as first-class citizens, the relevant numbers are the 0.67-0.79 band, not the 0.93 headline.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Better than most, and deliberately so: Trafilatura's own corpus is German-primary with 20-30% other languages including Chinese and Arabic, so it has been tuned against non-English input, and it auto-detects encoding rather than assuming UTF-8. Its length gates are still character-based, which under-counts information in CJK the same way Readability's do, and its XPath discard patterns are keyed on English and German class/id tokens (nav, footer, comment, kommentar, sidebar), so a site whose class names are in Japanese, Arabic or Cyrillic loses the negative half of the heuristic entirely and falls back to length statistics. No RTL-specific handling and no bidi isolation on output, so mixed-direction text is emitted without isolation marks and can render reordered. rs-trafilatura's classifier was trained on a predominantly English corpus (WCXB's own stated limitation), so its page-type predictions on non-English pages are untested -- and since extraction is conditioned on that prediction, a misclassification is a whole-page failure, not a gradual degradation. [uncertain] on the magnitude of that non-English classifier degradation; no one has measured it.
leaks_outward: As libraries, nothing: no telemetry, no phone-home, no analytics, and no network access at all in the extraction path. rs-trafilatura ships its XGBoost model as a compiled-in artifact, so there is no model download at runtime. The disclosure risk is entirely in the fetcher the caller pairs them with. Trafilatura's CLI does include a fetcher (urllib3-based, with an optional crawler/spider mode and sitemap/feed discovery), and that fetcher makes a fresh session-less request with a library-default User-Agent -- a distinct, linkable server-side signal that a page is being harvested rather than read. If the project uses only the extraction function against DOM already in hand, nothing leaks; if it uses the fetcher, it opens a second, differently-fingerprinted connection to the origin.
mechanism_detectability: Undetectable client-side and moderately detectable server-side. Neither tool runs in the page, patches any DOM API, touches attachShadow, opens a CDP session, or installs an extension, so a page cannot observe extraction at all -- there is no client-side signature. Server-side, the Trafilatura fetcher's default UA string, its lack of subresource requests, its TLS fingerprint and its request cadence in crawler mode are all trivially detectable, and several bot-management vendors classify it directly. The relevant conclusion for this project: the extraction step is detection-neutral and the risk lives entirely in whoever performs the fetch, which in this architecture is the user's own browser under the user's own session -- the favourable case.
countermeasures: For the library, nothing needs hardening. The countermeasures that matter run the other way -- sites defending against Trafilatura -- and they are effective: client-side rendering defeats it completely, paywall stubs distil cleanly into a teaser it reports as the article, decoy containers seeded with body-like class names capture its positive XPaths, and content split across dynamically-inserted containers evades both its cascade and its fallbacks. Trafilatura offers a `favor_precision` / `favor_recall` pair and a `no_fallback` switch as tuning knobs, plus an LRU-cache paragraph deduplicator; none of these are hardening in the privacy sense, they are precision/recall dials.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not measured in the terms this project needs, by anyone. The published numbers measure agreement with a human/LLM-drawn main-content span; none measures loss against the full capture. The nearest available proxy is WCXB's snippet pair: Trafilatura retains 69.5% of ground-truth content while admitting 6.6% boilerplate; Resiliparse retains 74.5% while admitting 22.8%. Read as a fidelity cost that is a 30.5% content loss against a curated target, and an unknown loss against a full capture, which is the number that would compare against the project's 80.9%-projection-versus-99.7%-capture gap. Affordance retention is not merely unmeasured but structurally zero, so the fidelity cost on the interactivity axis is total. There is also no stated control: the benchmarks compare tools to each other, never a tool to the unextracted page.
gate_state_at_capture: Not recorded, not representable, and actively corpus-poisoning. Neither tool has a field for consent-banner state, paywall state, login-wall state or CAPTCHA interstitial. Cookie-consent containers are discarded by XPath pattern when the pattern matches and silently kept as body text when it does not, so a consent overlay's copy can land in the extracted 'article'. Paywall teasers extract cleanly and are reported as full articles with no flag. WCXB does not report gate state for its 2,008 pages either, so a benchmark that includes gated captures is scoring extractors against whatever the annotator saw behind the same gate, with no way to separate the populations afterwards. Given that roughly two-thirds of top sites present a consent interface, this is a silent stratification in every number quoted above.
determinism: Deterministic within a pinned version for Trafilatura: pure computation over an lxml tree, no randomness, no clock in the extraction path (dates are parsed from the document, not the system clock, though `htmldate`'s fallback heuristics can consult the current date when configured -- pin that off). The deduplication LRU cache is stateful across calls within a process, so running the same document twice in one process with `deduplicate` enabled can return less the second time; that is the one non-idempotency to guard. rs-trafilatura is deterministic given a fixed model artifact, but its determinism is conditional on the classifier: an XGBoost inference is deterministic, yet the extraction profile it selects is a discrete branch, so a page sitting near a decision boundary can flip its entire extraction between two near-identical inputs. That is a step discontinuity Python Trafilatura does not have.
determinism_across_versions: Output drifts materially. Trafilatura's XPath rule sets, discard patterns and fallback thresholds are revised in most minor releases, and the maintainer's own evaluation table is re-run and re-published per version, which is itself evidence that output moves. The lxml/libxml2 version underneath changes whitespace normalisation, entity handling and implied-element insertion, so the same bytes through two lxml builds are not the same tree. rs-trafilatura adds a second drift axis that is worse: the model artifact. Retraining the XGBoost classifier changes page-type predictions, which changes extraction profiles, which changes output on pages whose text did not change at all -- and there is no published model-version stamp in the output. Pinning must cover (trafilatura version, lxml version) or (rs-trafilatura version, model artifact hash) or reproducibility is not claimable.
reproducibility: Good for the tools, poor for the evidence. Given pinned versions and pinned input bytes, both tools re-produce their output exactly, and WCXB's release of HTML sources plus JSON ground truth under CC-BY-4.0 on GitHub/Zenodo/HuggingFace makes its ranking genuinely re-runnable -- a real strength, and better practice than Trafilatura's own evaluation set, which is described but whose composition is not released as a fixed public artifact. What is not reproducible is anything about the live web: both corpora are frozen HTML snapshots, which means they will age out of relevance (WCXB says so directly: 'temporal snapshot may not represent future web design'). This is the exact mirror of this project's problem -- WCXB is frozen and therefore stale; this project's 136 pages refetch live resources on 75% of reads and are therefore not frozen at all. Neither is the right answer; a pinned-capture-plus-live-refresh pair is.
failure_modes: (1) Client-rendered page yields the skeleton or empty string -- the dominant modern failure and completely silent. (2) Fallback cascade returns a different tool's opinion: when the primary XPath pass yields too little, output is actually readability-lxml's or jusText's, with no indication in the result which produced it, so downstream behaviour changes character without notice. (3) Wrong container selected on multi-column or multi-article pages, returning a rail or a related-stories block. (4) Comment thread promoted to body when comment XPaths do not match the site's markup. (5) Tables and code blocks flattened or dropped depending on output target -- Markdown and TXT lose things XML/TEI keeps, so the failure is target-dependent. (6) rs-trafilatura specific and severe: page-type misclassification applies the wrong extraction profile wholesale; a listing scored as an article, or vice versa, fails as a unit rather than degrading. (7) Encoding misdetection on pages with no declared charset, producing mojibake that still passes downstream length checks.
failure_visibility: Mostly silent, with one partial exception. Empty or near-empty output is detectable by the caller with a length check, and Trafilatura will return None when it finds nothing, which is loud enough to branch on. Everything else degrades silently: there is no confidence score, no field naming which cascade stage produced the text, no count of discarded nodes, no margin between the winning and runner-up container. rs-trafilatura is the better citizen here -- it ships an explicit extraction-quality predictor (a 27-feature XGBoost model that predicts the extraction F1) and exposes a confidence score, which is a genuinely useful and rare affordance and is the single mechanism from this item most worth copying. But note what it is: a model predicting another model's agreement with an LLM-drafted oracle. It is a calibrated guess, not a check, and it will be confidently wrong exactly where the classifier is confidently wrong.
scale_limits: Linear in document size with a low constant and genuinely fast: rs-trafilatura reports 71 files/s on articles and 45.8 files/s overall on the 1,497-page WCXB set with compile-time regex; Python Trafilatura is roughly an order of magnitude slower but still hundreds of pages per minute per core. Both are whole-document in memory with no streaming, so cost tracks total DOM size rather than kept-content size -- a chrome-heavy page costs the same as a prose-heavy one of equal node count. The fallback cascade is the superlinear risk in Python Trafilatura: a page that triggers the full ladder is parsed and scored up to three times by three different algorithms. Neither has a batch amortisation, an incremental mode, or any cross-document reuse; cost is strictly per page and never sublinear across a corpus.
delta_cost_model: There is none, in either implementation, and the architecture forbids one. Both are whole-document functions from bytes to text: every extraction re-parses the entire document and recomputes global statistics (text/link ratios, container scores, and in rs-trafilatura's case a 181-feature vector over the whole page) before any output is produced. A single character change costs a full re-run. Every change class falls outside any delta bound: text edits, attribute changes, subtree insertion, shadow mutation (invisible to it entirely), CSS-driven change (invisible), canvas (invisible), and declarative shadow DOM in the initial parse (parsed as inert template markup and either dropped or emitted as literal template content -- a specific, checkable wrong behaviour worth testing against). rs-trafilatura is strictly worse than Python Trafilatura here because its classifier is a whole-page feature vector, so even a hypothetical incremental extractor would still need a full-page featurisation pass to know which profile to apply. This is the direct negation of o_delta and useful only as the whole-page control against which a delta claim is timed.
reanchoring_stability: No node identity is carried at any point, so there is no re-anchoring and no re-anchor rate to measure. Output elements carry no xpath, no source offsets, no ids (stripped), and no content hashes; the XML/TEI target preserves element TYPE but not element IDENTITY, so two runs over two versions of a page can only be compared by diffing text, which conflates a DOM move with a content edit. Trafilatura does carry a document-level url in its metadata and TEI header, which is one level of address -- better than Readability's nothing, and exactly one component of this project's url:xpath:markdown:content key. The xpath component, which is the one that makes re-anchoring possible, is absent. Against W3C Web Annotation dual selectors or content-defined-chunking boundaries, both tools sit at the floor.
adversarial_exposure: Exposed, and in a specific asymmetric way. Attribute-level concealment (hidden, aria-hidden, inline display:none) is caught by the discard XPaths. Everything requiring computed style is not: an external stylesheet class that hides a div, off-screen absolute positioning, zero-height clipping, zero font-size, and background-matched colour all survive into the output if the concealed text sits inside the selected container. Because neither tool reads layout, neither can filter concealment without layout, which is exactly the structural exposure this project has -- so Trafilatura is NOT a safer comparison point, it is the same exposure with less capture. Its accidental defence is deletion volume: it throws away most of the page, so most injected payloads land in discarded regions. That defence inverts completely for a payload placed inside the article body, which is the placement an attacker who has read the extractor's source would choose. One additional exposure specific to this family: Trafilatura's metadata extraction reads JSON-LD, Open Graph and meta tags -- attacker-controlled fields -- and promotes them to first-class output fields (author, title, sitename, license), providing a clean high-trust injection channel that the prose-only extractors do not have.
provenance_carrying: Document-level only, and thin. The best case is XML-TEI output, whose teiHeader carries source url, title, author, date, sitename, license and hostname -- so a persisted artifact knows where it came from and roughly when it was published. There is nothing per token, per paragraph or per element: no xpath, no character offsets into the source, no capture timestamp distinct from publication date, no shadow depth (the concept does not exist), and no gate state. The publication date is parsed from the page, so it is attacker-controlled and is NOT a capture time. For the per-token origin that current prompt-injection defences require, Trafilatura supplies roughly one field of the four this project's trie key already supplies for free. The TEI header pattern is nonetheless worth copying as a serialization convention for the document-level half.
roundtrip_safety: Not a fixed point, and not designed to be. Feeding Trafilatura's own Markdown or TXT output back through Trafilatura yields a different, usually smaller result: the transform destroys the class names, link densities and container contrasts its own heuristics depend on, so the second pass has no signal to work with. The XML/TEI target is closer to idempotent because it is a typed tree, but round-tripping it through the HTML parser is not defined behaviour. Escaping policy in the Markdown target is the standard weak spot -- literal characters that are Markdown syntax in the source text (pipes inside table cells, leading hashes, underscores, backticks) are a known source of structure corruption in this whole tool class, and a fixed-point test over the Markdown target is a cheap oracle-free fidelity metric that nobody in this space publishes. Neither tool claims XSS-safe sanitization; script and style are removed but the guarantee is not stated as security-grade.
token_budget_and_ordering: No budget concept, no truncation policy, and no ordering contract. Output is document order of the selected container, and the caller owns every downstream decision about what to cut. There is one relevant lever: Trafilatura's `favor_precision` / `favor_recall` switches shift the aggressiveness of the discard pass, which is a crude global size dial but not a ranked budget -- it cannot say 'keep the most valuable 4k tokens', only 'keep less' or 'keep more'. Nothing in either tool has a notion of which content is highest value, so where the important material lands in a model's context is whatever the page author decided. Past the 50% context-fill point where position bias turns recency-dominant, that is an uncontrolled variable, and a fold that has an ordering contract is strictly better here regardless of extraction quality. rs-trafilatura's confidence score is the one signal that could feed a budget policy: it lets a caller spend more context on pages the extractor believes it handled well, which is a defensible ordering heuristic even though it is not one the tool implements.
representation_cost: Typically a 90-98% reduction against source HTML byte count on an article, and roughly 5-20% of source token count -- comparable to Readability but with more structure retained per token because headings, lists and tables survive. The XML/TEI target costs perhaps 20-40% more tokens than the TXT target and buys typed structure plus a metadata header; Markdown sits between them and is the sensible default for SLM context. What is bought per token saved is the same total loss as Readability on the axes this project cares about: all affordances, all interactive state, all addressability, all shadow content, and the entire non-selected surface of the page. The compression is achieved by deletion, so it does not trade back -- there is no dial that recovers a dropped control.
what_could_be_adopted: Four mechanisms, none of them the extraction algorithm. (1) The XML-TEI output convention -- a typed element tree plus a provenance header -- as the model for the fold's serialization: it demonstrates that structure and document-level provenance can coexist in one artifact, and TEI's element vocabulary (head/p/list/item/table/row/cell/quote/code/graphic) is a ready-made, structure-agnostic tag set that names shapes rather than regions. (2) rs-trafilatura's extraction-quality predictor and exposed confidence score: the PATTERN is the adoptable part -- emitting a per-capture self-assessment alongside the artifact so downstream consumers can branch on it -- even though its particular model is not, since it predicts agreement with an LLM oracle this project does not have. Emit an oracle-free equivalent instead: recall against capture, round-trip fixed-point delta, and unreachable-node count. (3) The multi-format output discipline: one extraction, several serializations (TXT/MD/XML/JSON), which maps directly onto the markdown-plus-ASCII-wireframe dual rendering. (4) Trafilatura's per-tool published, versioned, re-runnable evaluation table as a practice -- re-run per release, published with the version number and date -- which is the frozen-control discipline the project's live-refetching corpus lacks. What must NOT be adopted: the XPath discard patterns and the page-type classifier, which are the disqualifying parts.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: REJECTED for both, and rs-trafilatura more severely. Trafilatura's positive and negative XPath sets are region classifiers by construction (nav, footer, sidebar, comment, aside, share). rs-trafilatura escalates this into an explicit trained classifier that names the page a forum, a product, a listing or an article and then branches extraction on that name -- the paradigm case of the forbidden move, and worse than a heuristic because the naming is now a model whose decision boundary is opaque. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS for both. Neither reads geometry at any stage; there is no rendering engine in the pipeline, and rs-trafilatura's 181 features are structural/lexical counts, not geometric. This is the one constraint the family satisfies cleanly. o_delta: REJECTED for both, rs-trafilatura strictly worse. Whole-document parse plus global statistics per call, with a whole-page feature vector gating the branch in the Rust version; every change class is outside any bound, and shadow/CSS/canvas changes are not merely outside the bound but invisible. no_mocks: NEUTRAL to NEGATIVE. As pure transforms they introduce no stub surface, but rs-trafilatura embeds a trained model artifact in the measured path, which is a frozen approximation of a judgement and would need version-stamping to stay honest under a no-mocks reading. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY. Neither touches attachShadow, so neither violates the rule -- but neither traverses open shadow roots either, and neither emits an unreachable marker, so both silently under-report shadow content and would score well on a benchmark while missing the components entirely. That is the dishonest-coverage behaviour the constraint exists to prevent. OVERALL VERDICT: Trafilatura -- negative oracle only, with the TEI serialization and evaluation discipline extractable. rs-trafilatura -- rejected as a component; adoptable in the actuator layer only, and only for its confidence-score pattern, never its classifier.
governance_signal_handling: Partial and fetcher-scoped. Trafilatura's spider/crawler mode and its sitemap/feed discovery do read and honour robots.txt (via urllib3 plus a robots parser), and the CLI exposes politeness controls (delay, per-host throttling). That is the extent of it: there is no Content Signals parsing, no ai.txt support, no IETF AIPREF vocabulary implementation, no Web Bot Auth signature or Signature Agent Card, and no HTTP 402 handling path -- a 402 is simply an error status. rs-trafilatura has no fetcher at all and therefore no governance surface whatsoever. Since access is increasingly governance-determined rather than merely governance-regulated, neither tool can be cited as a compliance story; for this project the fetch is the user's own browser under the user's own session, so the obligation sits with the user's normal browsing, and adopting either library contributes nothing either way.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The libraries retain nothing; the caller's persisted artifact is the regulated act under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026. What they hand you to persist is unhelpfully PII-rich: author names are extracted and promoted to a first-class metadata field, comment threads are extracted deliberately by a dedicated pass (user-generated content with a materially different privacy expectation than editorial copy), and any personal data inside the body text is retained verbatim with no redaction pass. No gate-state marker and no capture timestamp are recorded, so a legitimate-interest balancing test over a Trafilatura-built store has no data to work from and cannot distinguish a public article from a logged-in view of someone's forum posts. The data-minimisation argument has to be made entirely outside the tool. One point in its favour: `include_comments=False` is a single switch that removes the largest UGC surface, and it is a cheap, defensible default that this project should mirror as an explicit stored flag rather than an implicit setting. [uncertain] on how EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 specifically treat extracted-and-stored author metadata as distinct from body text; that distinction is not settled in the guidance I could verify.
